title: Fish Tacos Baja
subtitle: beer-battered white fish in corn tortillas with slaw and crema
excerpt: Baja-style fish tacos are built around crisp beer-battered white fish tucked into warm corn tortillas with a sharp white cabbage slaw and a lime crema. The batter is light and thin. The fish inside stays moist. This is quick street food you can make at home in under an hour.
sourceNotes: Fish tacos are associated with the Baja California peninsula, particularly the city of Ensenada, where fried fish tacos became street food staples in the mid-twentieth century. The beer batter is a signature element of the Baja style.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Mexican cultured cream similar to creme fraiche but slightly thinner and milder. Sour cream thinned with a little lime juice makes a good substitute.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 40 minutes from start to eating. The fish is 600 g of firm white fish such as cod or haddock. The beer batter is made with 200 ml of light lager, which keeps it crisp without making it heavy.

The oil temperature is critical. Too cool and the batter soaks up oil and turns greasy. Too hot and it browns before the fish is cooked through. Aim for 180°C and fry in small batches so the temperature does not drop.
Make the crema. Mix the sour cream with the juice of 1 lime and a pinch of salt until smooth. Thin with a splash of water if it is too thick to drizzle. This is your

Make the slaw. Shred about 200 g of white cabbage as finely as you can. Toss with the juice of the second lime and a pinch of salt. Leave to sit while you prepare the fish. The lime softens the cabbage slightly.
Cut the 600 g of cod or haddock into strips about 2 cm wide and 8 cm long. Pat completely dry with kitchen paper. Season with salt.

Make the batter. Put the flour into a bowl with half a teaspoon of salt. Pour in 200 ml of cold light lager and whisk until just combined. A few lumps are fine. Do not overwork the batter. Keep it cold.

Pour oil to a depth of 3 cm into a large, deep frying pan. Heat over medium-high heat to 180°C. If you do not have a thermometer, drop a small piece of batter into the oil. It should rise to the surface immediately and start bubbling.

Dip each piece of fish into the batter, letting the excess drip off briefly. Lower gently into the oil. Fry 3 to 4 pieces at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper. Keep warm in a low oven while you fry the rest.

Warm the corn tortillas in a dry pan or over a flame. Build each taco with a pinch of slaw, a piece of fried fish, a few slices of avocado, a few rings of jalapeño and a drizzle of crema. Serve immediately.

attrs.symptom: The batter is greasy and does not crisp up.
attrs.cause: The oil was not hot enough when the fish went in.
attrs.fix: Let the oil return to 180°C between each batch. If you add too many pieces at once, the temperature drops too far.

attrs.symptom: The batter slides off the fish.
attrs.cause: The fish was wet when it went into the batter.
attrs.fix: Pat the fish very dry with kitchen paper before dipping. Moisture prevents the batter from sticking.

attrs.symptom: The tacos are soggy by the time they reach the table.
attrs.cause: The fish was dressed too early, or the slaw was not drained.
attrs.fix: Assemble tacos just before eating. Drain the slaw of any excess lime juice before adding.

content.text: Fish tacos come from Baja California, the long peninsula on Mexico's Pacific coast. Ensenada is the city most closely linked to this dish. The tacos are sold from stands near the harbour. The beer batter and the slaw are the two defining elements. This is casual, fast food that is good on a warm evening.
